title: Diwali

jokes.text: Nice dress, Ryan. / It's not a dress, it's a kurta.
jokes.setup: Ryan shows up to work wearing traditional Indian clothing — something completely unexpected from the intern/temp.
jokes.punchline: Someone calls it a dress; Ryan corrects with 'kurta' — he knows exactly what it is and wears it earnestly, which is funnier than if he were embarrassed.
jokes.explanation: Clean quick joke that establishes Ryan's awkward over-investment in Kelly's life. The correction with the proper term lands because Ryan says it with defensively earnest confidence — he's wearing it, he's committed, and he knows the word. Sets up the Ryan/Kelly dynamic efficiently.

jokes.text: Tonight, one of our most ethnic co-workers, Kelly...
jokes.setup: Michael begins a talking-head about Diwali, positioned as if he's delivering thoughtful cultural commentary.
jokes.punchline: 'One of our most ethnic co-workers' — the phrasing is so casually wrong that it reframes Michael's entire attempt at inclusivity as its own offense.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. 'Most ethnic' is a phrase that couldn't come from any other character — it's Michael trying desperately to be inclusive while demonstrating he has no idea what that means. The adjective 'most' implies ethnicity is a spectrum and Kelly ranks highly on it. It's specific, it's character-perfect, and it lands with the cringe weight that only Michael can generate. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Michael mimics Kelly: 'It's... I have... It's so super fun and it's gonna be great.'
jokes.setup: Michael frames this as Kelly's actual cultural explanation of Diwali.
jokes.punchline: The impression is pitch-perfect and devastating — Kelly's explanation really IS this vapid, which makes Michael simultaneously right and condescending.
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels — Michael is mocking Kelly while simultaneously revealing his own condescension, and the impression foreshadows that Kelly genuinely won't know much more than this. Character integration is strong: only Michael would do a mocking impression of his employee on camera while thinking he's being charming.

jokes.text: A lot of gods with unpronounceable names. Twenty minutes later you find out that it's essentially a Hindu Halloween.
jokes.setup: Michael is ostensibly educating his employees about an important religious holiday.
jokes.punchline: 'Hindu Halloween' — Michael reduces a major religious festival to the most accessible American analogue he can find, delivered as if this is actually helpful.
jokes.explanation: 'Hindu Halloween' is a genuinely funny coinage — it sounds like Michael actually sat with someone for 20 minutes and this was his takeaway. The 'twenty minutes later' implies a journey toward understanding that ends in spectacular failure. Character-specific and quotable.

jokes.text: Phyllis or another female coworker fawning over Ryan in his kurta: 'You look so handsome. You really do.' / 'How come you didn't get me one?'
jokes.setup: Ryan arrives in traditional Indian dress and a coworker gushes over him.
jokes.punchline: The follow-up 'How come you didn't get me one?' reveals she wants one too — treating it like a gift-giving occasion, completely missing the point.
jokes.explanation: Functional background joke that gets a smile. The 'get me one' line shows the coworker's obliviousness but it's not sharp enough to really land. Works as texture.

jokes.text: Angela's counter-offer to Diwali: 'Do you want to make Appletinis and watch Sex and the City at my place?'
jokes.setup: Someone says they might not go to Diwali.
jokes.punchline: Angela's alternative plan is deeply on-brand: prissy, aggressively un-hip, and presented as if this is the obviously superior option. Appletinis and Sex and the City as a rebellious counter-program.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character integration — this is quintessentially Angela. She's not anti-Diwali out of overt bigotry, she's just aggressively indifferent and has a very specific counter-proposal. The specificity of 'Appletinis' (trying to be fun) combined with 'Sex and the City' (mainstream safe choice) perfectly captures her character.

jokes.text: Pam says she doesn't have anyone to go with; Kevin suggests she go with Dwight because 'He's single too, right?' / 'Yeah, totally single. Hundred percent available.'
jokes.setup: Pam laments having no one to go to Diwali with.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's solution — Dwight — and Pam's overcorrecting endorsement of Dwight's availability ('Hundred percent available') suggests she's performing enthusiasm to deflect from the real issue (Jim).
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels for attentive viewers — Pam's 'Hundred percent available' is almost defensive, suggesting she's trying very hard not to say Jim's name. Rewatch bonus for the subtext. Kevin's obliviousness is consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Jim asks vaguely who's going to the Diwali event; another character immediately translates: 'Oh, you mean like, Is Pam going?'
jokes.setup: Jim asks casually who's going to Diwali.
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately cuts through the pretense — the whole office knows Jim's real question.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and economical. The joke is in the translator's instant accuracy — Jim's transparent crush is apparently visible to everyone. The casual matter-of-factness of the interpretation is funnier than any elaborate setup would be.

jokes.text: Creed: 'Don't go. They eat monkey brains.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks about the Diwali event.
jokes.punchline: Creed delivers a confident, completely fabricated racist warning about monkey brains with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: Peak Creed. The joke works because it's absolutely characteristic — Creed states something insane as casual fact, with no apparent awareness or apology. 'They eat monkey brains' is delivered like he's tipping off a friend about a restaurant's bad parking. The economy is perfect — four words, total commitment. Nearly scores 8 because it's character-specific and economical, but falls just short of the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Michael corrects Creed: 'Indians do not eat monkey brains. And if they do, sign me up because I am sure that they are very tasty and nutritional.'
jokes.setup: Michael intervenes to defend Indian culture from Creed's offensive claim.
jokes.punchline: Michael's defense immediately collapses into 'sign me up' — he undermines his own correction by expressing enthusiastic interest in the fictional practice.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Michael comedy. The structure is perfect: he starts as the righteous defender ('That is offensive'), which raises our expectation that he'll model correct behavior — then immediately pivots to 'sign me up.' The word 'nutritional' at the end is the killer — it sounds like a PSA endorsement for monkey brains. This joke justifies 8+ because the structure (setup/collapse/escalation), the character specificity, and the absurd final word are all working in concert. This is what Michael Scott does best.

jokes.text: Michael to Stanley: 'Come Kwanza time, I have got you covered, baby.' / Stanley: 'I don't celebrate Kwanza.' / Michael: 'Really? You should. It's fun.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to demonstrate he celebrates diversity, addressing Stanley specifically.
jokes.punchline: Michael assumes Stanley celebrates Kwanzaa because he's Black. Stanley corrects him. Michael doubles down with a recommendation.
jokes.explanation: Works beautifully as a three-beat joke. The assumption is Michael's racism in good intentions; the correction is Stanley's weary dignity; the 'Really? You should. It's fun.' doubles down with breezy confidence that makes it worse. 'It's fun' is a particularly rich beat — Michael has apparently done research on a holiday he assigned to Stanley.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I love the people here. And if there was one thing I don't really care for, is that they can be terribly, terribly ignorant about other cultures. And I don't want them embarrassing me in front of my girlfriend, Carole.'
jokes.setup: Michael frames himself as the culturally sophisticated one who must manage his employees' ignorance.
jokes.punchline: The reason he cares about cultural sensitivity is entirely self-interested — he doesn't want to look bad in front of his girlfriend, not because ignorance is actually wrong.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael self-revelation — he presents a noble motivation (concern about ignorance) that immediately collapses into vanity (his girlfriend). The irony is that we've just watched him be terrible with Stanley. Strong character integration: Michael is constitutionally unable to be motivated by anything other than his own image.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Kelly for his Diwali seminar with fanfare: 'Kelly, you are on!' — and Kelly's entire explanation is that it's 'awesome and there's food and there's gonna be dancing, and I got the raddest outfit.'
jokes.setup: Michael has built up the cultural seminar as important; Kelly is introduced as the resident expert.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's expert testimony is purely about her outfit, which validates Michael's earlier impression of her perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Payoff to the setup at 00:23 where Michael mimicked Kelly's vapid explanation. The joke is that Michael was completely right — she really is this shallow about her own cultural heritage — and also that this makes the seminar a complete disaster. Rewatch bonus because the callback lands harder the second time.

jokes.text: Michael asks Kelly 'How many gods do you have?' and she replies 'Like hundreds, I think, maybe more. I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is ostensibly the cultural expert being consulted.
jokes.punchline: She doesn't know basic facts about her own religion and answers with complete indifference ('I don't know').
jokes.explanation: Functional continuation of Kelly's cluelessness. 'Like hundreds, I think, maybe more' is a good approximation of someone who genuinely doesn't know but is trying to sound like they do. Works but is less sharp than the outfit line.

jokes.text: About the blue deity statue: 'And that blue, busty gal, what's her story? She looks like Pam from the neck down.' / Dwight: 'Pam wishes.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks about a Hindu goddess depicted in a statue.
jokes.punchline: He reduces the goddess to a comparison with Pam's body; Dwight's immediate 'Pam wishes' burns Pam while defending the goddess's honor, which he doesn't realize is absurd.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels — Michael's inappropriate sexualization of religious imagery, and then Dwight's snap defense of the goddess's body over Pam's without any awareness of how weird that is. 'Pam wishes' is a great line because Dwight is simultaneously insulting Pam and implicitly expressing admiration for a Hindu goddess. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Michael dismisses Dwight's accurate Diwali history: 'This isn't Lord of the Rings.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just given factually accurate historical/religious context for Diwali.
jokes.punchline: Michael compares it to fantasy fiction — ironically revealing that his cultural knowledge is so shallow he can't distinguish Hindu mythology from Tolkien.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — five words that perfectly encapsulate Michael's cultural illiteracy while he thinks he's being the sophisticated one in the room. The irony is thick: Dwight was correct, Michael's correction is wrong, and Michael has positioned himself all episode as the culturally aware one. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Jim arrives at work visibly sweaty from biking in, and delivers a talking head about how biking saves gas, keeps him in shape, helps the environment — 'and now I know it makes me really sweaty for work.'
jokes.setup: Jim lists the admirable benefits of biking to work, matching Josh from Stamford.
jokes.punchline: The final item — 'makes me really sweaty for work' — undercuts every previous virtue signal with a practical catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: Clean list-joke structure — three virtuous benefits followed by the embarrassing real-world consequence. Works as a Jim moment because it's played without ego; he's genuinely figuring this out in real time. The pause before the final item helps the delivery.

jokes.text: Someone comments on Jim's bike: 'Nice basket.' / Jim: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been embarrassed about being sweaty; a coworker notices his bike.
jokes.punchline: The comment targets the most emasculating detail (the basket), and Jim thanks them sincerely — either missing the dig or choosing not to fight it.
jokes.explanation: Small but efficient. Jim's 'Thank you' is the whole joke — genuine or ironic, it works either way. Economical and character-appropriate: Jim often responds to mockery by disarming it with earnestness.

jokes.text: Michael talking-head: 'There are literally billions of people just like Kelly in the world.'
jokes.setup: Michael frames Kelly as special and unique ('one in a million').
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts this by noting that statistically, she's one of billions — which is both accurate about world population and a brutal accidental insult.
jokes.explanation: Structurally clever — Michael tries to hold two thoughts simultaneously (Kelly is special / Kelly represents a billion people) without realizing they contradict each other. The phrase 'literally billions of people just like Kelly' is inadvertently dehumanizing. The 'but it's also not true' pivot is the structural key.

jokes.text: Michael's 'Famous Indians' slideshow: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar ('Impressive'), then Apu from The Simpsons ('Hilarious Indian').
jokes.setup: Michael is presenting famous Indians as cultural education.
jokes.punchline: He lists a Nobel Prize-winning physicist alongside a fictional cartoon character, treating them with equal legitimacy.
jokes.explanation: The pairing of Chandrasekhar and Apu is the joke — Michael apparently found them through the same search and presents them as equivalent cultural ambassadors. 'Hilarious Indian' as Apu's descriptor is particularly good: it reduces him to one adjective while also being mildly accurate. The structure implies Michael sorted by 'impression' level (Impressive / Hilarious) rather than any relevant criteria.

jokes.text: Michael lists M. Night Shyamalan, names his films, then delivers the Sixth Sense spoiler ('He was dead the whole time') and says 'Just stop it.'
jokes.setup: Michael is listing famous Indians, reaches M. Night Shyamalan.
jokes.punchline: He spoils The Sixth Sense completely unprompted — to a room of people — and then addresses the audience directly ('Just stop it') as if they're the ones who caused this.
jokes.explanation: The spoiler is funny, but the 'Just stop it' directed at no one in particular is what elevates this — Michael seems to be addressing the film itself, or perhaps his own brain, for making him remember the twist. Works as a peek into Michael's chaotic thought process.

jokes.text: Jim asks Karen to help retrieve his stuck vending machine chips with her 'skinny little arms.'
jokes.setup: Jim approaches Karen with a task.
jokes.punchline: His phrasing — 'skinny little arms' — is oddly personal for an office context; Karen's slightly amused 'Oh' suggests she notices but doesn't mind, which establishes their dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as relationship establishment — Jim and Karen are flirtatious in a workplace-appropriate way. Rewatch bonus because knowing what develops between them makes this scene richer. The joke itself is mild but the dynamic it signals is important.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head about Karen: 'We have such a roller-coaster thing, Karen and I... Roller-coastery friendship. Hot and cold, on again, off again, sexual tension-filled type of deal. It's very Sam and Diane.'
jokes.setup: Jim is describing his relationship with Karen to the camera.
jokes.punchline: He self-corrects from 'roller-coaster thing' to 'roller-coastery friendship' when he realizes what he almost said — then immediately describes everything that makes it NOT just a friendship, ending on 'Sam and Diane.'
jokes.explanation: The self-correction mid-sentence ('Excuse me? Roller-coastery friendship') is a great character beat — Jim catching himself almost admitting feelings and awkwardly backing up. Then he describes the relationship in terms that confirm exactly what he denied. The Sam and Diane reference is smart for a character who positions himself as culturally aware.

jokes.text: Michael pivots from Sam and Diane to: 'And another thing about the Indian people, they love sex positions. I present to you the Kama Sutra.'
jokes.setup: The meeting cuts from Jim's romantic musing back to Michael's cultural seminar.
jokes.punchline: Michael introduces the Kama Sutra as a cultural educational exhibit with the same tone as a corporate PowerPoint.
jokes.explanation: The tonal mismatch is the joke — 'they love sex positions' delivered with the earnestness of a TED Talk. The transition from the seminar context makes it land harder because he's treating this as equivalent to the Chandrasekhar slide.

jokes.text: Kevin identifies the 'Union of the Monkey' position immediately: 'I have, that's Union of the Monkey.'
jokes.setup: Michael holds up the Kama Sutra and asks who's seen it before.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's immediate, specific, confident identification of the position by its name.
jokes.explanation: Kevin knowing the name 'Union of the Monkey' with that confidence is perfectly in character — he would absolutely have done this research. The specificity is key; if he just said 'I've seen that' it would be nothing. The name itself is also funny.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'This is the best meeting we have ever had.'
jokes.setup: The room is looking at the Kama Sutra during a company meeting.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's genuine enthusiasm, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Eight words and perfect character economy. Kevin's standards for a good meeting are purely hedonistic, and the fact that he's comparing this to other meetings — and Dunder Mifflin meetings are legendarily awful — gives the line unexpected depth. His sincerity is the whole joke.

jokes.text: Michael talks about Toby collecting the Kama Sutras: 'My Indian cultural seminar was going great until Toby decided he was too immature to deal with culturally explicit images.'
jokes.setup: Toby has shut down the Kama Sutra portion of the seminar.
jokes.punchline: Michael's confessional completely inverts responsibility — Toby is 'too immature' for pulling sexually explicit material from a workplace meeting.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael inversion of blame — the person behaving appropriately is cast as the immature one. The phrase 'culturally explicit images' is a wonderful Michael Scott coinage that frames pornographic material as anthropology. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: My Indian cultural seminar was going great until Toby decided he was too immature to deal with culturally explicit images.
jokes.setup: Michael is doing a talking-head about the Kama Sutra seminar.
jokes.punchline: Michael has completely inverted the situation: it was HIS seminar that was inappropriate, and he assigns immaturity to Toby for objecting. 'Culturally explicit images' as his euphemism for pornography is delicious.
jokes.explanation: Strong Michael confessional. 'Culturally explicit images' is a perfect euphemism that only Michael would deploy — it has the rhythm of a PR phrase but the content of a self-serving rationalization. His projection of immaturity onto Toby is in perfect keeping with his inability to perceive himself accurately.

jokes.text: Michael: 'It's just sex, people, everybody does it. I'm doing it with Carole probably tonight.'
jokes.setup: Michael is defending the Kama Sutra as cultural material.
jokes.punchline: He announces his sex life to his employees as supporting evidence, with the word 'probably' undermining his confidence immediately.
jokes.explanation: 'Probably tonight' is the key word — it signals that Michael isn't as certain about this as he's performing, which makes the overshare worse. He's shared too much AND it might not even be true. The fact that Carole turns him down later in the episode makes this retroactive foreshadowing.

jokes.text: Once a quarter, the sales staff of this branch has to stay late to do order form consolidation which, amazingly, is even less interesting than it sounds.
jokes.setup: Jim explains the reason the sales staff (including Karen) is staying late and can't go to Diwali.
jokes.punchline: 'Amazingly, is even less interesting than it sounds' — the self-aware acknowledgment that 'order form consolidation' is already the least compelling description imaginable, and somehow the reality is worse.
jokes.explanation: Solid Jim deadpan. 'Amazingly, is even less interesting than it sounds' is well-phrased — the 'amazingly' sets up the impossible and delivers. A good texture joke that captures the soul-crushing reality of corporate life in Jim's resigned style.

jokes.text: Jim in the Stamford office, alone while everyone's at Diwali: 'You guys ready to party!' — greeted by the empty, silent office.
jokes.setup: Jim is stuck at Stamford doing order consolidation; he tries to rally the team.
jokes.punchline: His enthusiasm meets dead silence — he's the only one who tried, and possibly the only one there.
jokes.explanation: Solid visual/situational joke about Jim's isolation at Stamford — he's physically separate from the main plot and the visual of him trying to make a boring task fun and failing is characteristically Jim. Inferred from the dialogue and scene structure.

jokes.text: At the Diwali celebration: 'Isn't this fun? Not wearing shoes?' — someone who apparently has a foot disease responds: 'Stop it. It's a disease. I told you.'
jokes.setup: Guests are removing shoes at the Diwali event.
jokes.punchline: One person has apparently been warned not to go barefoot due to a contagious foot condition — the casual delivery of 'It's a disease' in this context is unexpectedly dark.
jokes.explanation: Funny because of what it implies — someone brought a foot disease to a sacred cultural space where shoes are removed. The 'I told you' suggests this was actually warned against. Dark and specific in the way Office humor often is.

jokes.text: Kevin arrives in an elaborate Indian costume: 'I thought you said this was a costume party.' / Michael: 'What does that look like to you?' / Kevin: 'An Indian woman in a sari.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is apparently dressed in full costume at a Diwali celebration where no one else is in costume.
jokes.punchline: Kevin explains he thought it was a costume party — and when challenged, correctly identifies his costume as 'An Indian woman in a sari' without embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Kevin in a sari is the primary comedy, but what elevates it is Kevin's matter-of-fact self-description. He's not embarrassed; he thought this was appropriate. His description is technically accurate, which somehow makes it funnier. Character-specific: Kevin does not sweat small things.

jokes.text: Michael surveys the Diwali food — 'Now these are limes, lemons, onions...' — then announces he's vegetarian and asks what he can eat. When told it's all vegetarian: 'I'll just have some bread.'
jokes.setup: Michael attends a vegetarian-friendly cultural feast.
jokes.punchline: He defaults to bread — the blandest, most culturally unengaged choice possible — at a table full of elaborate food he won't try.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Michael's cultural performance collapsing at the food table — he's told everyone how open and appreciative he is, but his actual behavior is to seek the whitest possible option at an Indian feast. 'I'll just have some bread' lands because of the specific cowardice it represents.

jokes.text: Michael eats food with his hands at the Diwali celebration in a way that apparently horrifies the hosts: 'You used your hands.' / 'Oh, yuck, oh...'
jokes.setup: Michael is navigating the food at Diwali.
jokes.punchline: He does something so wrong with his hands that the hosts — people from a culture that often eats with hands — are disgusted. The specifics aren't clear but the reaction is.
jokes.explanation: Mostly visual joke that's limited by being a transcript — we can't see what Michael did. The payoff 'Oh, yuck, oh...' suggests he did something uniquely offensive but we can only infer. Loses impact without the visual.

jokes.text: Michael tries something, is asked if it's too spicy, then reveals: 'These s'mores are disgusting.' / 'They're not s'mores, they're samosas.' / 'Do you think they have any s'mores?'
jokes.setup: Michael has been eating something he thinks is a familiar food.
jokes.punchline: He's been calling samosas 's'mores' — the phonetic similarity apparently fooled him — and after being corrected, he asks if they have the actual thing.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Three-beat structure is perfect: (1) Michael hates what he's eating, (2) revelation that he's misidentified it through phonetic confusion, (3) he asks for the thing he actually wanted, still not engaging with the Indian food at all. The detail that he ate multiple of them hating them before this moment is implied and adds depth. The follow-up 'All they are is chocolate, graham cracker and marshmallow. How difficult would that have been?' is an almost-funny extension that actually dilutes slightly, but the core joke is excellent. Justifies 8+ for originality and character integration — this specific mistake could only happen to Michael.

jokes.text: Do you think they have any s'mores? All they are is chocolate, graham cracker and marshmallow. How difficult would that have been?
jokes.setup: Michael has just been corrected that he's been eating samosas, not s'mores.
jokes.punchline: He doubles down, not just asking if there are s'mores but explaining the recipe as if the hosts failed to provide something extremely simple. His sense of entitlement — explaining to Kelly's family how easy s'mores are to make — is the cringe escalation.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the previous joke. Michael explaining s'mores as if it's the hosts' oversight is perfectly entitled. 'How difficult would that have been?' is a great punchline word — he's genuinely baffled that a Hindu cultural celebration didn't include American campfire snacks.

jokes.text: Ryan approaches Kelly's sisters; they speak to him in Hindi, and Kelly screams at them: 'Rupa, Neepa, Tiffany, stop acting like such little losers and just be cool!'
jokes.setup: Ryan tries to make conversation with Kelly's sisters at the celebration.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's sisters mock him in Hindi; Kelly's reaction reveals the name 'Tiffany' among the traditional names ('Rupa, Neepa, Tiffany') — an unexpected break in the pattern — and her scolding them to 'be cool' is mortifying.
jokes.explanation: 'Tiffany' is the joke within the joke — the pattern of traditional Indian names suddenly interrupted by an extremely American name. Kelly screaming at her sisters in front of Ryan to 'be cool' is classic Kelly self-sabotage. The family dynamic is efficiently established.

jokes.text: Kelly's sisters apparently say something to Ryan about Zach Braff.
jokes.setup: Kelly's sisters have been speaking Hindi to Ryan.
jokes.punchline: Ryan reports back that they mentioned Zach Braff — suggesting the sisters find Ryan attractive in a Zach Braff way, which is funny given Ryan's own self-image.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny detail — Zach Braff is an unusual touchstone for Kelly's sisters to invoke, and the randomness of it works. But it's a throwaway and relies heavily on the visual of Ryan's reaction.

jokes.text: Pam shows up to Diwali: 'I feel a little underdressed, but at least I'm not dressed like a slutty cheerleader, right? Is that mean?'
jokes.setup: Pam arrives at the Diwali celebration.
jokes.punchline: She takes a shot at an unnamed woman in a cheerleader costume (Carol/Carole, Michael's girlfriend), immediately second-guessing herself with 'Is that mean?'
jokes.explanation: Pam being casually catty and then catching herself is a great character beat — she's not usually the barbed one. The 'Is that mean?' undercuts it perfectly, showing she's aware she's stepping out of character. The descriptor 'slutty cheerleader' also retroactively sets up the Carole/Michael conversation about the costume.

jokes.text: Dwight spots Ryan across the Diwali party and yells 'Temp! Temp!' while chasing him down.
jokes.setup: Ryan is trying to navigate the Diwali party independently.
jokes.punchline: Dwight treats 'Temp!' like a hunting call — he refers to Ryan only by his job classification even at a social event, suggesting Ryan has no identity beyond his title for Dwight.
jokes.explanation: Extremely character-specific — Dwight's relationship with Ryan has always been defined by rank and classification. The urgency of 'Temp! Temp!' as if flagging a cab or a running dog is perfect Dwight. The social context (a party) makes the hierarchical insistence funnier.

jokes.text: Kelly's parents try to set up Kelly with a doctor named Vali while Ryan stands there: 'Ryan is a temporary worker. Makes no money. Vali is a whole doctor, so handsome. Makes good money.' / Kelly: 'Do you think I want to date a doctor?'
jokes.setup: Kelly's parents are openly trying to set her up with a more suitable match at the party, with Ryan present.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's defense of Ryan isn't 'I love him' but 'Do you think I want to date a doctor?' — which implies she's thought about this and rejected it for petty reasons.
jokes.explanation: The cringe works because Ryan has to stand there while being described as 'temporary worker, makes no money' — an accurate but brutal assessment. Kelly's counter-argument is also funny because she doesn't claim to love Ryan; she just refuses the alternative. The mother's 'a whole doctor' phrasing is a nice character detail.

jokes.text: Andy and Jim take shots together at the Diwali party: 'One, two, three, shot!' followed by Andy's extended reaction: 'Oh, holy mother of God... Oh, that burns! Golly... That's good...'
jokes.setup: Andy and Jim are drinking together.
jokes.punchline: Andy's over-the-top reaction to a shot — including 'holy mother of God,' 'burns,' 'Golly,' and then 'That's good' — is a full emotional journey through one shot's aftermath.
jokes.explanation: Andy's verbal over-reactions are a character signature. 'Golly' amid profanity is a specifically Andy contradiction. Sets up his later drunkenness. The extended emotional journey of a single shot — from horror to appreciation — is character-specific and visually implied.

jokes.text: Kelly's dad asks Michael how long he's been with his 'cheerleader' girlfriend; Michael corrects that she's not a cheerleader, she 'thought this was a costume party.'
jokes.setup: Kelly's family is getting to know Michael at the party.
jokes.punchline: The dad has already categorized Carole as 'the cheerleader,' and Michael's correction — that she thought it was a costume party — is somehow more embarrassing than just accepting the label.
jokes.explanation: Payoff to both the 'costume party' misunderstanding and Pam's earlier observation. The fact that Michael defends Carole by explaining the costume-party confusion doesn't help her case — it makes the situation stranger, not better.

jokes.text: Wow! Thirty years. And you two only met once before the wedding night? / Yes. Wow. / How long have you been married to the cheerleader?
jokes.setup: Michael is talking to Kelly's parents about their arranged marriage and expressing genuine admiration for their thirty-year marriage.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's father immediately turns the question around by asking about 'the cheerleader' — referring to Carol in her cheerleader costume — delivering both a callback to the costume situation and an implied judgment of their unconventional relationship.
jokes.explanation: Nice reversal — Michael is performing cultural curiosity and the parent pivots to question HIS relationship with the same directness. 'The cheerleader' as shorthand is both funny and slightly cutting. Sets up the next beat well.

jokes.text: Kelly's dad: 'She is very fair.' Michael agrees enthusiastically: 'Very fair and very kind.' — Dad meant skin tone.
jokes.setup: Kelly's dad compliments Carole.
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets 'fair' as a personality trait (just/kind) while the dad clearly means skin complexion — revealed by the repeated 'very fair' emphasis.
jokes.explanation: Clean double-meaning joke that works on first watch and rewards second viewing. Michael's enthusiastic agreement ('Very fair and very kind') is oblivious and slightly endearing — he's receiving what he thinks is a compliment about his girlfriend's character while the dad is making a colorism comment. The show doesn't over-explain it.

jokes.text: Kelly's dad asks Michael: 'So, tell me, is your marriage the kind of thing where when you die, she has to throw herself on a fire?'
jokes.setup: Kelly's dad is making polite conversation with Michael about his relationship.
jokes.punchline: He asks about sati (widow self-immolation) as casually as one might ask about a prenuptial agreement.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark-comedy inversion — the episode has been about American characters being ignorant of Indian customs, and here an Indian character casually references a historical practice as if it's current and standard. The casualness of delivery is the key — 'throw herself on a fire' said with the same energy as asking about vacation plans. Sharp and subversive.

jokes.text: Michael: 'No, okay. It's still very cool. Okay, thanks.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just been asked if his girlfriend will have to throw herself on a fire when he dies.
jokes.punchline: Michael's response — declining while still calling the practice 'very cool' so as not to offend — is social cowardice wrapped in cultural appreciation.
jokes.explanation: The 'It's still very cool' is the joke — Michael won't criticize anything about Indian culture even when the correct response would be to simply say 'no, that's not a thing.' His performative open-mindedness won't let him reject even historical widow-burning. Character-perfect.

jokes.text: Michael's public marriage proposal speech: 'I know you're all thinking, Who is this crazy gringo and what is he talking about? Well, I'm not crazy. Maybe I'm crazy in love.'
jokes.setup: Michael grabs the microphone to make an announcement at the Diwali celebration.
jokes.punchline: His self-characterization ('crazy gringo') and pivot ('Maybe I'm crazy in love') are both deeply Michael — he's performing a rom-com moment at someone else's religious holiday.
jokes.explanation: 'Gringo' is not a word Michael would organically reach for — he's clearly been rehearsing this and thought that word would resonate with an Indian audience. The self-awareness of 'crazy' immediately redirected to 'crazy in love' is Michael's movie-brain at full throttle. The character integration is excellent: only Michael hijacks someone else's religious celebration to propose to a girlfriend of 9 dates.

jokes.text: Carol says 'Can we talk about this in private?' (twice, because Michael doesn't hear); Michael says 'I didn't hear you?' — then the mic thud as she has to do it again.
jokes.setup: Michael has just proposed publicly; Carol is trying to decline gracefully.
jokes.punchline: Michael forces her to say 'Can we talk about this in private?' twice — the first time not hearing it on a microphone, which means everyone heard it the first time except him.
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent cringe — Carol is trying to minimize the public embarrassment by asking for privacy, but Michael makes her repeat herself into a live mic, making it MORE public. The structural irony is clean and painful. The mic thud that punctuates her second request is a perfect physical beat.

jokes.text: After Carol rejects the proposal: 'This is our ninth date, Michael.' / Michael: 'Well, yeah. But I... I feel like I've known you many lifetimes. Maybe I'm Hindu after all. Okay, I'm not Hindu, but...'
jokes.setup: Carol has just rejected Michael's proposal and explained it's only their ninth date.
jokes.punchline: Michael's deflection goes: reincarnation joke, claim he might be Hindu, immediate retraction. He's spinning wildly.
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe I'm Hindu after all. Okay, I'm not Hindu, but...' is a great Michael spiral — he reaches for the context around him (Diwali, Hinduism) as a romantic argument, then immediately abandons it. The speed of the retraction ('Okay, I'm not Hindu') is the comic key. Only Michael converts to Hinduism for 1.5 seconds as a relationship strategy.

jokes.text: I feel like I've known you many lifetimes. Maybe I'm Hindu after all. Okay, I'm not Hindu, but...
jokes.setup: Carol has pointed out it's only their ninth date; Michael is trying to explain his emotional logic.
jokes.punchline: Michael invoking reincarnation to justify his proposal and immediately walking it back ('Okay, I'm not Hindu') in the same breath. The self-correction arrives so fast it suggests even he didn't fully commit to the idea.
jokes.explanation: Michael reaching for reincarnation as his romantic metaphor at a Diwali celebration is perfectly on-brand — he's absorbed exactly one piece of Hindu philosophy and applied it to his collapsing proposal. 'Okay, I'm not Hindu' as an immediate disclaiming of the very idea he just used is a good comedic rhythm.

jokes.text: As Carol leaves, Michael tries to come with her: 'Hey, you know what? Why don't I come with you? 'Cause I've got this book called the Kama Sutra...'
jokes.setup: Carol has rejected Michael's proposal and is leaving.
jokes.punchline: Michael's final attempt to salvage the evening involves the Kama Sutra — which he collected from his own workplace meeting earlier.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback that rewards episode attention. Michael earlier announced he'd 'probably' be sleeping with Carole; he earlier showed the Kama Sutra at a workplace meeting. Now he brings the book to a rejected proposal exit as a Hail Mary. The desperation, the callback, and the character are all aligned. 'Good night, Michael.' is Carol's perfect, tired response.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head with Kelly's family: 'Well, I was a temp, but I got promoted. So the compensation is a lot more competitive.' / 'So you're saving money now to start a family and home?' / 'Oh, or travel? And buy an Xbox.'
jokes.setup: Kelly's parents are interviewing Ryan about his future prospects, implying serious intentions.
jokes.punchline: Ryan pivots from 'family and home' to 'or travel? And buy an Xbox' — revealing his actual life plan.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure (saving money / family and home / Xbox) is clean and the final beat is perfect. Ryan adds 'or travel' as a buffer before 'buy an Xbox' — he knows how this sounds but he can't help himself. The Xbox specificity dates the episode but also makes it feel authentic. Strong character integration: Ryan is exactly the kind of guy who would say this.

jokes.text: Well, I was a temp, but I got promoted. So the compensation is a lot more competitive. / So you're saving money now... / ...to start a family and home? / Oh, or travel? / And buy an Xbox.
jokes.setup: Kelly's parents are interviewing Ryan about his financial prospects and future plans — the classic arranged-marriage family vetting, applied to this very un-arranged situation.
jokes.punchline: The parents build to 'start a family and home?' suggesting a responsible future; Ryan adds 'or travel?' as a more casual but acceptable answer, and then undercuts everything with 'And buy an Xbox.' The Xbox lands as the definitive statement of Ryan's actual priorities.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating structure is perfect: the parents are asking a serious question about Ryan's future; 'start a family and home' is the expectation; 'or travel' is a relaxed alternative; 'And buy an Xbox' is the complete deflation of Ryan's pretense of maturity. The 'and' implies it's not instead of those things, it's in addition — as if an Xbox is on the same list as starting a family. Perfect character: Ryan is trying to impress this family while accidentally revealing he's a 20-something kid. Well above the 8.0 anchor — this is an exceptional comedic structure.

jokes.text: Kelly's family asks if there's anything Ryan wanted to ask them; Ryan asks: 'Can you believe that my boss proposed to his girlfriend in public? That is so Michael. Is it?'
jokes.setup: Kelly's parents have created an obvious opportunity for Ryan to ask for Kelly's hand or express serious intentions.
jokes.punchline: Ryan completely misreads the moment and gossips about Michael's proposal instead — 'Is it?' suggests he's not even sure it is 'so Michael,' showing he barely knows his own boss.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection — the setup couldn't be more obvious (the perfect opportunity to propose) and Ryan swerves completely into gossip. 'Is it?' as a self-correction is the killer detail: he's not even confident in his own observation. The moment captures Ryan's emotional unavailability, his obliviousness, and his relationship with Kelly all at once. Strong structure.

jokes.text: Can you believe that my boss proposed to his girlfriend in public? / That is so Michael. / Is it? / He's really outgoing, huh? / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Ryan is apparently making small talk with Kelly's parents, mentioning Michael's proposal disaster.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's parents' response 'That is so Michael' — they apparently know Michael well enough to find his behavior completely predictable. Their framing of it as 'outgoing' rather than inappropriate is a gentle cultural-comedy beat.
jokes.explanation: Light callback that works as a grace note. 'Really outgoing' as a euphemism for Michael's behavior is a gentle joke. Ryan's 'Is it?' — questioning whether the proposal is 'so Michael' — is a small deadpan beat. Not strong enough to stand alone but earns its place.

jokes.text: Pam and Roy have a tense exchange at the party: she invites him to dance, he declines to watch the shoes, asks who she was texting. She says 'No one.' Phone buzzes immediately.
jokes.setup: Pam and Roy are at the Diwali party together, ostensibly trying to reconnect.
jokes.punchline: Pam says she wasn't texting anyone; her phone immediately buzzes — an almost perfectly timed contradiction.
jokes.explanation: The phone buzz is perfectly timed comedy-of-discomfort — the universe itself seems to call Pam a liar in front of Roy. Rewatch bonus because knowing it's Jim texting (likely) makes the scene richer. The 'who were you texting / no one / [BUZZ]' structure is simple and effective.

jokes.text: Andy performs a cappella at the party; Jim shuts him down: 'Andy, no a cappella.' Andy continues anyway, and somehow Jim joins in.
jokes.setup: Andy begins spontaneously singing at the Diwali celebration.
jokes.punchline: Jim tries to stop him, Andy ignores it, and Jim — despite his objection — gets pulled in and starts singing along.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jim's resistance collapses — the Indigo Girls song is apparently infectious enough to break his better judgment. Andy's immunity to discouragement is consistent with his character. The fact that they're singing 'Closer to Fine' at an Indian cultural celebration adds an absurdist layer.

jokes.text: (ANDY AND JIM SINGING together) / Wait. / The less I seek my source / Oh, come on, guys, please. / The closer I am to fine / That's not good. / Tuna! Are you kidding me?
jokes.setup: Andy has been told no a cappella; Karen thought she'd shut it down.
jokes.punchline: Jim joins in the singing, Karen's appeals escalate from resigned ('Wait') to exasperated ('Oh, come on, guys, please') to disbelief ('That's not good') to the specific betrayal of Jim participating ('Tuna! Are you kidding me?'). Jim's defection from the straight-man role is the twist.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the a cappella sequence. Karen's escalating reactions are perfectly calibrated — each line is funnier than the last. 'That's not good' as she watches Jim join is a great deadpan. 'Tuna! Are you kidding me?' — using Jim's Andy nickname — shows Karen is now entangled in Andy's world, which is its own joke. Jim joining the a cappella subverts his usual role as the sensible one, which is what makes it surprising.

jokes.text: After the a cappella, someone passes food that burns: 'Wow. That's so spicy. Here.' / Michael's distinctive exclaim.
jokes.setup: The group is eating at the Diwali celebration.
jokes.punchline: Michael's food reaction — likely an involuntary exclamation — marks another failed encounter with Indian cuisine.
jokes.explanation: Another food-reaction joke that adds to the running thread but doesn't add new information. Functions as texture and continuity rather than a standalone joke. Without the visual of Michael's reaction it loses significant impact.

jokes.text: Michael approaches Pam after being rejected: 'Pam, when Carole said No tonight, I think I finally realized how you must be feeling. We're both the victims of broken engagements.' / Pam: 'Well, you were never really engaged.' / Michael: 'I was in that marriage arena, though.'
jokes.setup: Michael is consoling himself after the failed proposal by finding a kindred spirit.
jokes.punchline: Pam correctly notes he was never engaged; Michael counters with 'I was in that marriage arena' — a phrase so desperate and specific that it earns its own category.
jokes.explanation: 'I was in that marriage arena, though.' This justifies 8+ comfortably. 'Marriage arena' is a Michael Scott coinage that is simultaneously recognizable (he means he was serious about someone) and completely insane (no such concept exists). The phrase implies marriage is a competitive venue — an arena — that he was adjacent to. The structure is perfect: Pam delivers a clean, accurate correction, and Michael's response accepts the correction while inventing a worse concept. It's quotable, character-specific to the point that no one else could say it, and concise. This is one of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Michael to Pam: 'I kind of thought something would happen tonight, too.' — pause — 'So alike.'
jokes.setup: Michael is sharing his disappointment about Carol with Pam, who is there nursing her own romantic disappointment.
jokes.punchline: 'So alike.' — Michael decides he and Pam are kindred spirits in romantic disappointment, which is both touching and deeply wrong.
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'So alike' is everything — it's Michael landing on this conclusion with genuine emotion, and the flat delivery of two words makes it oddly moving and also absurd. Michael's belief that he and Pam share a spiritual connection in romantic suffering is one of those Michael moments where his delusion and his genuine feeling coexist.

jokes.text: Michael attempts to kiss Pam; Pam rejects him: 'I'm rejecting your kiss.' / Michael: 'I... What? I didn't...'
jokes.setup: Michael has decided he and Pam have a 'so alike' connection and makes a move.
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'I'm rejecting your kiss' is so direct and clear that it leaves no room — and Michael's sputtered denial that he was going to kiss her is transparently false.
jokes.explanation: Justifies 8+. 'I'm rejecting your kiss' is an unusually formal and precise thing to say — Pam uses legal-document language in a moment of intense awkwardness, which is both funnier and more effective than any screaming or dramatic reaction would be. The formality is the punchline. Michael's 'I... What? I didn't...' sputter is a perfect follow, because he very clearly was. This is great Office cringe — the kind where Pam handles it with more dignity than Michael deserves.

jokes.text: Michael asks Pam for a ride home; Pam: 'If you sit in the back.'
jokes.setup: After the failed kiss attempt, Michael needs a ride.
jokes.punchline: Pam's condition — back seat only — is a perfectly calibrated punishment that simultaneously accepts and demotes.
jokes.explanation: Economy is near-perfect — five words that communicate Pam's stance completely without any drama. She's not refusing to help him; she's just making clear exactly where he stands. The implication is that the back seat is for children or pets, which is exactly the relational demotion he's earned.

jokes.text: Jim to Dwight: 'Hey, can I have a ride, man? I have my bike.' / Dwight: 'No way, dude. I am not driving home. I brought an inflatable bed for just such occasions. You're welcome to share it, though. It's a roomy twin.'
jokes.setup: Jim asks Dwight for a ride home from the party.
jokes.punchline: Dwight has pre-planned for the possibility of not driving home — he brought an inflatable bed, and it's specifically a 'roomy twin' — and invites Jim to share it.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Dwight — he prepares for every contingency, has planned ahead for getting drunk at a party by bringing emergency sleeping equipment, and the 'roomy twin' specification suggests he's thought about whether it could accommodate a guest. His offering to share without any social awareness of what this means is perfect. Nearly justifies 8 on character integration alone — this joke couldn't come from anyone else.

jokes.text: Drunk Andy stumbles out, and Karen yells: 'Hey, dummy, get in the car.' / Andy: 'I'm a drunk driver.' / Karen: 'Yes, you are.'
jokes.setup: Andy has gotten very drunk and needs to be managed.
jokes.punchline: Andy identifies himself as 'a drunk driver' with the confidence of someone who has reached a genuine self-realization; Karen confirms it flatly.
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'I'm a drunk driver' is said with zero self-awareness about the admission — he's narrating his condition, not confessing a crime, and the phrase happens to be a crime. Karen's 'Yes, you are' accepts this completely without missing a beat. Economy is excellent: the exchange is six words of dialogue total and perfectly captures both characters.

jokes.text: Hey, dummy, get in the car. / I'm a drunk driver. / Yes, you are. / Here, let me take that thing. Just get in the car.
jokes.setup: Carol has come back to give Michael a ride home after rejecting his proposal.
jokes.punchline: Michael's announcement 'I'm a drunk driver' — stated as a condition rather than a confession — and Carol's flat 'Yes, you are' acknowledgment. Carol has returned to take care of the man who just embarrassed her publicly. The absurdity of the situation (she's taking care of her failed proposer) is the backdrop.
jokes.explanation: Michael stating 'I'm a drunk driver' as if announcing a relevant fact rather than confessing a crime is good character comedy. Carol's 'Yes, you are' — agreeing without judgment — is an unexpectedly soft response from someone who just rejected him publicly. The 'Hey, dummy' opener is also warmly derogatory in a way that suggests their dynamic.

jokes.text: Andy in the car: 'And I am just going to lie down in the back, if that's all right?' — Karen: 'Sure. Here's your bag. Just don't puke on anything.'
jokes.setup: Andy is being driven home in a diminished state.
jokes.punchline: Karen's 'Just don't puke on anything' is a completely reasonable and maternal instruction that she delivers with casual authority.
jokes.explanation: Solid beat. Karen's handling of Andy has the competent resignation of someone who's done this before, which tells us something about her. The specific request 'don't puke on anything' is the right level of specificity — 'anything' rather than 'the seats' suggests she's given up on narrowing it down.

jokes.text: Michael in the car: 'These are not my shoes.'
jokes.setup: Michael is in the car after the Diwali event where shoes were removed.
jokes.punchline: He's apparently wearing someone else's shoes and has only just noticed — or is revealing this casually as if it's an afterthought.
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly because they're so understated. The callback to the shoe removal at the beginning of the party pays off here — Michael navigated the entire event, a failed proposal, a rejected kiss, and a car ride, and only now mentions the shoes. The timing of the revelation is the joke.

jokes.text: Michael starts to compare his car ride to 'Taxicab Confessions'; Pam: 'If you say one more word, I'm stopping the car.'
jokes.setup: Michael is in Pam's back seat trying to process his night.
jokes.punchline: Pam's threat is calm, final, and leaves no room — she's at her limit and communicating it with complete clarity.
jokes.explanation: Pam as Michael's exasperated handler is a reliable dynamic, and 'If you say one more word, I'm stopping the car' is the adult version of what you say to a child. Michael's 'Sorry' suggests he takes it seriously, which tells us something about how much Pam can actually control him when she's decisive.

jokes.text: Michael's Diwali song — a parody of Adam Sandler's Hanukkah song structure, sung to 'Indians everywhere': 'Diwali is a festival of lights / Tonight has been one crazy night / So put on your saris / It's time to celebrate Diwali / Everybody looks so jolly / but it's not Christmas, it's Diwali...'
jokes.setup: After an emotionally disastrous night, Michael takes the mic again to perform a tribute song.
jokes.punchline: The song is an Adam Sandler Hanukkah Song pastiche — Michael's solution to cultural appreciation is to imitate another minority's famous cultural song. The rhyme scheme is aggressively forced ('jolly' / 'Diwali'), and the line 'Don't invite any zombies to a celebration of Diwali' is the peak absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The Hanukkah song parody works because it's Michael's form of genuine tribute — he's thought about this enough to write a song, and the result is enthusiastic, clumsy, and oddly sweet. 'Don't invite any zombies to a celebration of Diwali' is a line with no logic that somehow scans. 'Along Came Polly to have some fun at Diwali' is a film reference with no justification beyond the rhyme, which is perfect Michael. Character integration is strong: this is Michael's love language.

jokes.text: In the Diwali song: 'The goddess of destruction, Kali / stopped by to celebrate Diwali'
jokes.setup: Michael is listing who came to celebrate Diwali in his song.
jokes.punchline: He includes Kali — the goddess of destruction — as a party attendee, which is both theologically confused and oddly festive.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Michael has done just enough research to know Kali exists, but not enough to understand why inviting the goddess of destruction to a festival would require context. He treats her like any other guest. Surprisingly charming.

jokes.text: In the Diwali song: 'Don't invite any zombies to a celebration of Diwali'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving advice about Diwali celebrations.
jokes.punchline: Zombie-exclusion as a Diwali tip has no cultural basis — Michael apparently needed a rhyme and landed on 'zombies.'
jokes.explanation: Purely absurdist — 'Don't invite any zombies to a celebration of Diwali' functions as advice with exactly zero cultural grounding. It exists entirely to rhyme with 'Diwali' and Michael has committed to it as practical guidance. The confidence of the warning is the joke.

jokes.text: In the Diwali song: 'Along Came Polly to have some fun at Diwali'
jokes.setup: Michael is listing attendees at Diwali.
jokes.punchline: The Jennifer Aniston/Ben Stiller film 'Along Came Polly' is name-dropped purely for the rhyme, given no justification within the song's logic.
jokes.explanation: Michael's Diwali song is clearly constructed backward from available rhymes — 'Along Came Polly' is here because 'Polly' rhymes with 'Diwali,' not because the film has any cultural connection. This is the Shyamalan reference strategy applied to songwriting. Works as a piece of Michael's creative process.

tmdb_overview: Michael was educating the entire staff about Diwali, the Hindu holiday that Kelly celebrated. Kelly had invited everybody from work to the celebration. Pam was unsure if she was going to make it, she later confided in Angela that she was saddened because she had nobody to attend the celebration with.
